chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Jaham ibn Humayd, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Where were you?' So I thought that he (peace be upon him) knew the place, so I said, 'May I be sacrificed for you! I was passing by so-and-so, so he withheld me, and I entered into his house and looked at his slave girls.' So he (peace be upon him) said to me: 'That is a gathering Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not Look at its inhabitants. May there be safety from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, upon your family and your wealth.'

key_terms.أَمِنْتَ اللَّهَ: May you be safe from Allah / May there be safety from Allah
key_terms.فُلَانٍ: so-and-so (a placeholder name for an unspecified person)
key_terms.مَجْلِسٌ: a gathering or session; here used metaphorically for a state or condition of being

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual consequence of entering a house and looking at slave girls according to Imam al-Rida?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) illustrates the spiritual peril of *ghurrah* (casual, unguarded gaze) by recounting his encounter with a companion who entered a home and viewed the slave girls. The Imam identifies this state as a *majlis* (gathering or condition) where Allah does not bestow His merciful gaze (*nazar*) upon the inhabitants, highlighting how visual indulgence can lead to a loss of divine favor and spiritual vigilance. This serves as a foundational principle in Shia jurisprudence regarding the ruling on looking at non-mahram women, emphasizing that the danger lies not just in the act itself but in the resulting spiritual negligence.
